title: Shiva's drum and the sounds of Sanskrit
hookLine: a story says the sounds of Sanskrit came from Shiva's drum; why Hindus treat the sound of a mantra itself as holy
carry: a mantra is holy sound, not just meaning
tomorrow: why does the dancer hold fire?
last: DARSHAN: TO SEE AND BE SEEN.

cards: A street vendor in Varanasi holds up a little drum shaped like an hourglass, two small heads joined at a narrow waist, two beads hanging on cords.
He twists his wrist back and forth, and the beads fly out and strike the heads, left, right, left, right, a fast rattling rhythm that carries down the lane. It's called a damaru.
Look up at Nataraja's upper right hand, and there it is, held between finger and thumb.

teach.h: THE DRUM: THE BEAT THAT STARTS IT.
teach.b: The drum is tied to sound, and in this tradition sound comes close to the beginning of things. Before anything is made, something is said, or struck, or sung.
So the drum in Nataraja's hand is read as the beat that starts the world, the rhythm the whole dance moves to. Grammarians tell a story about it.
At the end of Shiva's dance, the story goes, he sounded the damaru, and out came the sounds of the Sanskrit language, set out in short lists. Those lists are real.
They sit at the head of Panini's grammar of Sanskrit, and they're called the Maheshvara Sutras, the sutras of the great lord.

teach.h: A, I, U: THE FIRST LIST.
teach.b: The very first list begins with three vowels: a, i, u.
Whatever you make of the story, notice what it claims: the ordered sounds of a language, the building blocks of hymns and grocery lists alike, came from the rhythm of a dance.

And behind the story is a real Hindu teaching: sound itself can be sacred. The Vedas were carried for centuries by ear, teacher to student, every syllable kept exact. The Upanishads call the syllable Om Brahman itself.
So a mantra isn't only a message to God; the sound is part of the offering. That's why a grandmother corrects your Om Namah Shivaya, and why a chant in words you barely know can still fill a room.
Nataraja holds that beat up where everyone can see it. The dance starts here.

how: The damaru is played in Shiva temples and processions and by wandering devotees; students of Sanskrit learn the Maheshvara Sutras, which tradition links to Shiva's drum, and devotees chant Om Namah Shivaya, Shiva's five-syllable mantra, with care for every sound.

games.q: you're a student opening Panini's grammar of Sanskrit. before the rules begin, there are short lists of sounds. what does the old story say they are?
o: the sounds of Shiva's drum at the end of his dance.
the sounds of birds in the forest.
games.why: the story says they came from the damaru at the end of Shiva's dance. the lists are called the Maheshvara Sutras, the sutras of the great lord.

practice: Say Om Namah Shivaya, Shiva's five-syllable mantra, slowly, aloud or under your breath, and let each sound land before the next: na, mah, shi, vaa, ya.

Don't hurry toward the meaning; let the sound itself be the offering, the way the drum's beat comes before any word. If you don't pray, hum one long, low note and feel it in your chest, then listen to the quiet after it.
